title: Quarterly Business Review – Q3
transcript: Alex Morgan: Good afternoon everyone, and welcome to our quarterly business review for Q3. Thanks for blocking out the full afternoon, I know it's a lot of time. The plan is to go function by function, starting with finance, then sales, customer success, product and engineering, and marketing. We'll finish with risks and our priorities for Q4. Please keep questions coming as we go, this is meant to be a conversation rather than a series of presentations.
Tom Becker: Sounds good. Should I share my screen now?
Alex Morgan: Yes, go ahead Tom, the floor is yours.

Tom Becker: Great. Let me start with the headline numbers. We closed Q3 at four point two million dollars in annual recurring revenue. That's up from three point eight million at the end of Q2, so roughly ten and a half percent growth quarter over quarter. It's our strongest quarter so far in absolute terms.
Priya Shah: That's fantastic. How does that compare to the plan we set in January?

Tom Becker: We're slightly ahead. The plan assumed four point one million by the end of Q3, so we beat it by about a hundred thousand. Most of the upside came from expansion revenue rather than new logos.
Alex Morgan: Can you break down the movement in ARR for us?

Tom Becker: Sure. We added five hundred and twenty thousand in new and expansion ARR combined. Of that, about three hundred and ten thousand came from new customers and two hundred and ten thousand from expansions. We lost about one hundred and twenty thousand to churn and downgrades. So net new ARR was four hundred thousand.

Hannah Wright: The churn number is higher than I'd like, and I'll go into the details later. Two of the three churned customers were acquired by other companies, so it wasn't really about the product.

Tom Becker: Good context, thanks Hannah. Our net revenue retention for the trailing twelve months is now one hundred and twelve percent. That's up from one hundred and eight percent last quarter, which is a healthy sign that existing customers are growing with us.
Daniel Kim: What's driving the expansion? Is it mostly additional seats?
Tom Becker: Mostly seats, around seventy percent of expansion revenue. The rest is customers upgrading from the team plan to the business plan, usually for single sign on and advanced reporting.
Alex Morgan: Interesting. That tells us enterprise features are directly monetizable, which is relevant for our Q4 priorities.

Tom Becker: Exactly. Moving on to margins. Gross margin was seventy eight percent this quarter, up two points from Q2. The improvement mostly came from the infrastructure cost work Daniel's team did in July.
Daniel Kim: That was mainly moving our data sync workers to cheaper compute and cleaning up unused storage. We saved about eighteen thousand dollars a month.

Tom Becker: Which is real money at our size, so thank you. Now the less exciting part, spending. Our average monthly burn in Q3 was three hundred and ten thousand dollars. We have six point eight million in the bank, which gives us about twenty two months of runway at the current burn.
Priya Shah: Is twenty two months comfortable, or should we be worried?

Tom Becker: It's comfortable, but I'd like to keep it above eighteen months. That matters when we discuss hiring later. If we add every role on the wish list, runway drops to about sixteen months, which is below my comfort level.
Alex Morgan: Understood, we'll prioritize carefully. Anything else from finance before we move on?

Tom Becker: One more thing. Our accounts receivable is creeping up. We have about two hundred and forty thousand dollars overdue by more than sixty days, mostly from three customers. I'd like help from sales and customer success to chase those.
Hannah Wright: I can help with two of them, I have good relationships with their finance teams. Send me the list after the meeting.
Tom Becker: Will do, thanks Hannah.
Alex Morgan: Great, thanks Tom. Priya, over to you for sales.

Priya Shah: Thanks Alex. Q3 was a good quarter for new business. We closed fourteen new logos against a target of twelve. Our win rate improved to twenty seven percent from twenty two percent in Q2. I think a big reason is the new demo flow we introduced in July, which focuses on the customer's own data rather than our sample account.
Jordan Lee: That's great to hear. Is the demo flow something marketing can turn into a recorded demo for the website?

Priya Shah: Absolutely, let's talk after this meeting. The average deal size was about thirty one thousand dollars in annual contract value, which is slightly up from last quarter. Our sales cycle averaged forty eight days, which is about a week shorter than Q2.
Alex Morgan: What's behind the shorter sales cycle?

Priya Shah: Two things. First, the pilot program. Prospects who do a thirty day pilot decide faster and close at a much higher rate, around sixty percent. Second, having security documentation ready upfront. We used to lose two or three weeks waiting for security reviews.
Tom Becker: Is the pilot program costing us anything significant?

Priya Shah: Mostly time from customer success and solutions engineering. Each pilot needs roughly ten hours of support. Given the conversion rate, it's clearly worth it, but it does put pressure on Hannah's team.
Hannah Wright: It does. We ran nine pilots this quarter on top of normal onboarding. I'll come back to that when we talk about headcount.

Priya Shah: Now the harder part, losses. We lost eleven deals that reached the proposal stage. Six of those went to Lumen, mostly on price. Lumen is aggressively discounting, sometimes by forty percent, to win market share.
Alex Morgan: Are we losing on price alone, or are there feature gaps as well?
Priya Shah: Mostly price, but two prospects mentioned that Lumen has native Microsoft Teams alerts, and we only support Slack. For companies that live in Teams, that's a dealbreaker.
Daniel Kim: How big is that segment? Teams support isn't trivial, but it's also not huge once Slack alerts are done.
Priya Shah: Roughly a third of our pipeline uses Microsoft Teams as their main chat tool. Many of them haven't raised it yet, simply because alerts aren't launched.
Alex Morgan: That's a significant number. Daniel, let's get a rough estimate for Teams alerts before we finalize Q4 priorities.
Daniel Kim: Sure, I'll have a rough estimate by the end of next week.

Priya Shah: On pricing, I don't think we should match Lumen's discounts. Our win rate against them is still decent when the buyer cares about data quality. But I'd like us to do a proper competitive pricing analysis so sales has better guidance.
Tom Becker: I agree we shouldn't race to the bottom. I'm happy to support the analysis from the finance side, especially on what discount levels we can afford.

Priya Shah: Thanks Tom. Finally, the pipeline for Q4. We have about two point one million in weighted pipeline, which comfortably covers our new business target. The biggest opportunity is Northwind Traders, with eighty seats and a pilot starting soon.
Alex Morgan: I joined the Northwind discovery call this morning and it went really well. Their head of customer operations was very engaged, especially about Slack alerts.
Priya Shah: Yes, if Northwind closes it would be one of our largest new logos this year. I'm cautiously optimistic.
Alex Morgan: Great work, Priya. Hannah, let's move to customer success.

Hannah Wright: Thanks. I'll start with retention since we touched on churn earlier. We lost three customers in Q3, representing about one hundred and twenty thousand in ARR including downgrades. Two were acquisitions where the parent company already had a competing tool. The third was a mid-size customer who never fully adopted the product.
Tom Becker: Were there warning signs with the third customer?

Hannah Wright: Yes, in hindsight. Their weekly active users dropped by half over three months, and they skipped two of our quarterly reviews. We didn't have a systematic way to flag that, so we noticed too late.
Alex Morgan: That sounds like something we should fix with a health score.

Hannah Wright: Exactly, and that's one of my proposals for Q4. A simple account health score based on active users, dashboard views and support ticket sentiment. Any account that drops below a threshold gets a proactive outreach.
Daniel Kim: We have most of that data already. A first version could be a weekly report rather than a real-time feature.

Hannah Wright: A weekly report would be perfect to start with. Moving on, our net promoter score this quarter was forty six, up from forty one. The most common praise is the quality of our support and the speed of setup. The most common complaint is report customization.
Jordan Lee: Can I use the NPS comments in marketing materials if customers agree?
Hannah Wright: Yes, with permission. I'll share a list of promoters who are happy to be references.
Hannah Wright: Now onboarding. Our average time to value, meaning the time until a customer has their first dashboard in regular use, was nineteen days this quarter. My goal for Q4 is fourteen days.
Alex Morgan: What are the main delays in those nineteen days?

Hannah Wright: The biggest one is connecting data sources. Customers often need their IT team to approve the integration, and that can take a week. The second is training, especially for larger teams across time zones.
Alex Morgan: The product team is seeing the same thing in the onboarding checklist data. The data source step is where forty percent of self-serve users stall.
Hannah Wright: That's consistent. I'd love product and customer success to work on that together in Q4.
Alex Morgan: Definitely, let's make it a shared goal.

Hannah Wright: Last topic from me, team capacity. My team of four customer success managers handles ninety two accounts, plus the nine pilots this quarter. That's about twenty three accounts each, and the industry benchmark for our segment is closer to fifteen. We're stretched, and I'm worried about quality slipping on our top accounts.
Tom Becker: How many additional people would you need to get to a healthy ratio?
Hannah Wright: Ideally two, but one hire in Q4 would make a big difference, especially if the health score helps us focus.
Alex Morgan: Let's note that for the hiring discussion. Thanks Hannah. Daniel, product and engineering next.

Daniel Kim: Thanks. In Q3 we shipped two releases, 2.2 and 2.3. Release 2.2 included single sign on and SCIM provisioning, which Tom mentioned is already driving upgrades. Release 2.3 introduced the onboarding checklist and the new reporting engine. Release 2.4 with the redesigned dashboard and Slack alerts ships next Thursday.
Priya Shah: The single sign on release has been a big help in enterprise deals, so thank you.

Daniel Kim: Happy to hear it. On reliability, our uptime for the quarter was ninety nine point nine one percent. That's slightly below our target of ninety nine point nine five, mainly because of one incident in August.
Alex Morgan: That was the data sync outage, right?

Daniel Kim: Yes. A database migration locked a table that the sync workers depended on, and data sync was delayed for about three hours. No data was lost, but dashboards showed stale numbers during that time. We've since changed our migration process so large migrations run in batches during low traffic hours.
Hannah Wright: That incident generated quite a few support tickets. Customers appreciated the status page updates though, so communication helped.
Daniel Kim: Good to hear. We also introduced a formal postmortem process after that incident, and every action item from it has been completed.
Tom Becker: How is the team's velocity? Are we getting more done as the team grows?

Daniel Kim: Velocity is up about fifteen percent compared to Q2, measured in completed story points. But our CI pipeline has become flaky, which slows everyone down. Fixing the flaky tests is a priority for the next sprint.
Alex Morgan: What about hiring on the engineering side?

Daniel Kim: We filled two of our four open roles in Q3, a backend engineer and a data engineer. We're still hiring a senior frontend engineer and a site reliability engineer. We have a strong frontend candidate in the pipeline right now.
Alex Morgan: That's the candidate we interviewed together last week, right? I thought the interview went really well.
Daniel Kim: Yes, Marcus. I'm hopeful we'll make an offer soon.
Jordan Lee: From a marketing perspective, what's the most exciting thing coming in Q4?
Daniel Kim: Probably Slack alerts adoption and whatever we decide about Microsoft Teams. Also audit logs, which several enterprise prospects have asked for.
Priya Shah: Audit logs come up in almost every security questionnaire now. Having them would remove friction from enterprise deals.
Daniel Kim: Agreed. I'd estimate about four weeks of work for a first version of audit logs.
Alex Morgan: Thanks Daniel. Jordan, marketing's turn.

Jordan Lee: Thanks. Marketing generated one thousand eight hundred and fifty qualified leads this quarter, up twenty two percent from Q2. LinkedIn continues to be our best performing channel, both in volume and in lead quality.
Priya Shah: The leads from LinkedIn have definitely been the best quality on our side too. The webinar leads were also strong.

Jordan Lee: Right, we ran two webinars this quarter with about four hundred and fifty registrations in total. Around thirty percent of attendees requested a demo afterwards, which is our best conversion of any channel.
Tom Becker: What's our customer acquisition cost looking like?

Jordan Lee: Blended customer acquisition cost was about nine thousand four hundred dollars per new customer. With our average deal size, the payback period is roughly fourteen months. That's within the range we agreed on, but I'd like to bring it down.
Tom Becker: Fourteen months is acceptable, but if it creeps above eighteen I'd want to revisit the spend mix.

Jordan Lee: Understood. The plan for Q4 is to put more budget into webinars and customer stories, which are cheaper per lead than ads. We're also launching the 2.4 campaign next week, with the headline know about support spikes in minutes, not days.
Alex Morgan: I like that headline a lot. It came out of our brainstorm last week.
Jordan Lee: One request for everyone. We need more customer stories. Right now we have only two published case studies, and sales keeps asking for more, especially in specific industries.
Hannah Wright: I'll identify three or four happy customers who might agree to a case study. Globex could be a great one once they finish onboarding.
Jordan Lee: That would be amazing, thank you.
Alex Morgan: Thanks Jordan. Now let's talk about risks. What keeps each of you up at night?

Tom Becker: For me it's the runway versus growth trade off. If growth slows while we're increasing headcount, we'd need to raise money sooner than planned, and the fundraising environment is still difficult.
Priya Shah: My biggest risk is Lumen's pricing pressure. If they keep discounting heavily, our win rate could drop, especially in the mid-market.
Hannah Wright: For me it's team capacity. If we keep adding customers and pilots without adding people, quality will suffer, and that's when churn starts.
Daniel Kim: Reliability. As we grow, the data volumes grow too, and the August incident showed that we have some fragile parts. Hiring the site reliability engineer is important.
Jordan Lee: For marketing, it's dependency on LinkedIn. If their ad costs go up, our customer acquisition cost goes up immediately. We need to diversify.

Alex Morgan: These are all fair. I'll add mine, which is focus. We have more good ideas than capacity, and the risk is doing many things halfway. That's why I want us to agree on a short list of Q4 priorities today.

Alex Morgan: Here's my proposal for Q4. Priority one, launch 2.4 successfully and get at least forty percent of active workspaces using Slack alerts. Priority two, enterprise readiness, meaning audit logs and a decision on Microsoft Teams alerts. Priority three, cut time to value from nineteen days to fourteen. And priority four, reach four point seven million in ARR by the end of the year.
Tom Becker: Four point seven million is ambitious but achievable with the current pipeline. I'd keep it.
Priya Shah: I'm comfortable with that target, especially if Northwind closes.

Daniel Kim: Priority two worries me a bit. Audit logs plus Teams alerts plus supporting 2.4 is a lot for the team. Could we commit to audit logs and a Teams estimate, and decide on building Teams alerts in mid November?
Alex Morgan: That's reasonable. Let's commit to audit logs and make the Teams decision by mid November, once we have the estimate and better pipeline data.
Hannah Wright: For priority three, I'll need product time. Can we plan a joint project on the data source connection step?
Alex Morgan: Yes, I'll assign a product designer to work with you. Maria has done a lot of user research on onboarding recently, so she'd be a great fit.

Alex Morgan: Now hiring. We have requests for a customer success manager, a site reliability engineer, a senior frontend engineer and a product marketing manager. Tom, what fits within the runway guidance?

Tom Becker: If we add the senior frontend engineer, the site reliability engineer and one customer success manager, runway stays at about nineteen months. Adding the product marketing manager as well brings us to around seventeen months.
Jordan Lee: I can live without the product marketing hire until Q1 if the budget for webinars increases a little.
Tom Becker: I can support an extra forty thousand dollars for marketing programs in Q4. That's much cheaper than a full time hire.

Alex Morgan: Then let's approve three hires for Q4, the senior frontend engineer, the site reliability engineer and one customer success manager, plus forty thousand for marketing programs. We'll revisit the product marketing role in Q1.
Daniel Kim: That works for engineering.
Hannah Wright: Thank you, that will really help my team.

Alex Morgan: Great. Let me recap the action items. Tom will update the financial model with the approved hiring plan and share the overdue accounts list with Hannah. Priya will lead the competitive pricing analysis on Lumen with support from Tom. Hannah will build the first version of the account health score report with Daniel's team and identify case study candidates. Daniel will estimate Microsoft Teams alerts by the end of next week and scope audit logs. Jordan will plan the Q4 webinar calendar. And I'll write up the Q4 priorities and share them with the whole company by Monday.
Tom Becker: Sounds right to me.
Priya Shah: All good.
Alex Morgan: Thank you all. This was a strong quarter, and I'm really proud of the team. Let's make Q4 even better.

summary.gist: Acme closed Q3 at $4.2M ARR (+10.5% QoQ) and agreed on four Q4 priorities and three new hires.
summary.overview: The leadership team reviewed Q3 function by function. ARR reached $4.2M, about 10.5% above Q2 and slightly ahead of plan, with net revenue retention at 112%, gross margin at 78% and about 22 months of runway. Sales closed 14 new logos at a 27% win rate, while six late-stage losses went to the discounting competitor Lumen and Microsoft Teams alerts emerged as a gap. Customer success reported three churned accounts, an NPS of 46 and a 19-day time to value, and proposed an account health score. Engineering shipped releases 2.2 and 2.3 with 99.91% uptime, and marketing grew qualified leads 22%. The team agreed on four Q4 priorities and approved three hires plus $40k for marketing programs.
